details.description: Ink-2 is Cartesia's streaming speech-to-text model built for real-time voice agents, launched July 9, 2026. Cartesia describes it as its fastest and most accurate streaming STT, with native turn detection so agents know when a caller has finished speaking without a separate voice-activity-detection step. It accurately transcribes structured data such as phone numbers, dates, and emails, and is currently offered for English, French, Hindi, Japanese, and Spanish with automatic language detection.
advantages: Cartesia reports a 6.5% word error rate on live production calls, versus 9.2% for ElevenLabs Scribe and 9.4% for Deepgram in the same test.
On AppTek's 14-accent English benchmark, Cartesia reports an 8% word error rate for Ink-2, versus 10% for Deepgram Flux and 12% for ElevenLabs Scribe v2.
Native turn-detection events (turn.start, turn.eager_end, turn.end) use semantic endpointing that reads meaning rather than silence, so agents wait less and interrupt less.
Time-to-final-transcript of 0.1 seconds, with a turn.eager_end signal that lets an agent start generating a response before the final transcript is confirmed.
Natively parses structured data such as phone numbers, dates, and emails without extra post-processing.
Ranked #1 on Artificial Analysis's streaming speech-to-text leaderboard, per Cartesia.
disadvantages: Only supports realtime/streaming transcription endpoints; Cartesia's own batch transcription endpoint uses the older Ink-Whisper model instead.
Covers five languages (English, French, Hindi, Japanese, Spanish) versus the 99 languages of Cartesia's older Ink-Whisper model.
use_cases: Real-time conversational voice agents that need low-latency turn detection.
Any live application needing structured-data-aware transcription (phone numbers, dates, emails).

sources.title: Introducing Ink-2: The #1-ranked STT built for voice agents

notes: The launch blog post (Jul 9, 2026) says Ink-2 shipped English-only with 'multilingual support on the way'; the current docs page now lists five languages, which I used as the current state per the catalog facts' guidance to prefer current pages. WER figures are Cartesia's own reported comparisons, not a named third-party leaderboard, so I kept them out of the evaluations list (word-error-rate is explicitly not an accuracy score) and put them in advantages instead. The dated snapshot referenced in Cartesia's docs is unspecified beyond 'Ink 2'; no deprecation or preview status was found for it.
